nameStory: The vermilion flycatcher gets its name from its stunning bright red coloration, particularly striking in males. 'Vermilion' refers to the brilliant red-orange pigment that was historically made from crushed cinnabar mineral, perfectly describing this bird's fiery plumage that makes it stand out like a living ember among the generally drab brown and olive members of the flycatcher family.
description: The vermilion flycatcher is a small songbird that's a true showstopper among New England's typically modest-colored flycatchers. Males are unmistakable with their brilliant red crowns, chests, and bellies contrasting with brownish wings and tails. Females are much more subdued, wearing brownish plumage that can make identification tricky. These are aerial insectivores, meaning they catch flying insects on the wing, and they prefer open areas near water where insects are abundant.

idTips.label: Male Coloration
idTips.description: Adult males display an unmistakable bright vermilion-red crown, chest, and underparts that seems to glow in sunlight, contrasting sharply with dark brownish wings and tail

idTips.label: Female Appearance
idTips.description: Females wear subtle brownish plumage overall with lighter underparts and may show a peachy or salmon wash on the belly, lacking any bright red coloration

idTips.label: Hunting Behavior
idTips.description: Watch for their distinctive flycatcher habit of perching upright on exposed branches or wires, then darting out to snatch insects mid-flight before returning to the same perch

idTips.label: Song
idTips.description: Males sing a distinctive 'pit pit pit pidddrrrreeedrr' that starts with sharp notes and trails into a trilled ending, often delivered from a prominent perch

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: Small, compact flycatcher with a relatively large head, straight black bill perfect for catching insects, and an upright posture when perched

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Found in semi-open areas near water sources like streams, ponds, or wetlands where they can easily spot and catch flying insects

habitat: In New England, vermilion flycatchers are extremely rare visitors typically found in semi-open habitats near water sources such as pond edges, stream corridors, or wetland margins. They prefer areas with scattered perches like fence posts, dead snags, or utility wires overlooking open ground where they can hunt for flying insects. When they do appear, it's usually in riparian areas or parks with water features and mixed open and wooded terrain.

seasonality.spring: Peak time for any New England sightings, typically during migration when lost birds may appear. Males would be in full breeding plumage showing their brightest red coloration.
seasonality.summer: Extremely rare but possible, especially early summer. Birds may be completing their molt which begins in summer, potentially making identification more challenging.
seasonality.fall: Occasional vagrant records during fall migration. Males may show somewhat duller red plumage as they begin or continue their molting process.
seasonality.winter: Virtually absent from New England as these birds retreat to warmer southern regions. Any winter sighting would be exceptional and noteworthy.

funFact: Despite being socially monogamous, vermilion flycatchers are quite the cheaters - they regularly engage in extra-pair copulation and females sometimes practice 'brood parasitism' by sneaking their eggs into other vermilion flycatcher nests, letting other parents raise their young!
confusionNotes: Female vermilion flycatchers can be confused with Say's phoebes, which also have brownish plumage and similar size. Look for the vermilion flycatcher's slightly more compact build, straighter bill, and any hint of peachy coloration on the underparts. Remember: if you see bright red, it's definitely a male vermilion flycatcher - no other New England flycatcher comes close to that coloration.
contextualKnowledge: Vermilion flycatchers are so rare in New England (only 15 recorded observations) that any sighting would be considered a significant vagrant event worth reporting to local birding communities and eBird. These are birds that belong in the southwestern United States and Central/South America, so finding one in New England represents a truly exceptional occurrence.
compareHints: Vermilion flycatchers are the only members of their genus, making them unique among flycatchers. Compared to other tyrant flycatchers in New England like phoebes, pewees, and Empidonax flycatchers, vermilion flycatchers are the only ones with any bright red coloration in males. Even the females can be distinguished by their more compact build and the subtle peachy tones that other regional flycatchers lack entirely.
